Parasuramesvara Temple

Mukteshvara Temple

Parasuramesvara Temple is about 2.9 m taller than Mukteshvara Temple — about 1.3× as tall.

Parasuramesvara Temple
Date
c. 7th–8th century CE (debated) Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,2,3,4]

Note: No foundation inscription is known, so every date comes from style or letter shapes. Panigrahi (1961): the first or second part of the 7th century, about 650 CE. Brown (1959): towards the end of the 8th century, from its style and outside influences; he adds that the shrine may have been added after the hall. R.D. Banerji (reported by Panigrahi): not earlier than the 8th century, from the letter shapes of the planet labels on the door. Mitra (1880): 9th century, because its workmanship and stone match the Mukteshvara and Rajarani. Fergusson (1876): about 500 CE, using the traditional Kesari king list; otherwise he would have said 450 CE.

Dynasty
Shailodbhava period (debated) Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,4]

Note: This rests on Panigrahi's own date of about 650 CE, which other scholars dispute (see date). Fergusson (1876) suggested it 'may belong to the preceding dynasty', before his Kesari kings. No source names the person who paid for it.

Height
about 13 m (44 ft) Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [2]

Note: Only one height was found in the sources checked: Brown (1959), 44 ft for the tower. He gives 48 ft for the length of shrine and hall together. This is not an ASI measurement. Panigrahi gives no figure, and Fergusson gives only the plan, about 20 ft square. Mitra's description may give a size, but that part could not be read. Other figures circulate, but their sources were not checked.

Deity
Debated: Shiva or Vishnu Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,3,4]

Note: Panigrahi (1961) notes carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Mitra (1880) reports that the Ekamra Purana calls its god Daityesvara, and he reads some porch panels as scenes from Rama's life. Fergusson (1876) judged it Vaishnava from its name and wall carvings. No source checked says outright which god is worshipped here today.

Temple type
Not yet verified — see our content policy.

What's special

Its porch hall (jagamohana) is well preserved. It lets scholars study the early form of this hall. A raised central roof and stone windows with carved holes let light in. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,2,3]

Note: The sources give different numbers of doors for the hall (Panigrahi two, Brown three), so no count is given.

On the shrine doorway is a carved slab of planet gods, with their names inscribed beside them. Panigrahi noted that early temples like this one leave out Ketu, the ninth planet. Later temples such as Mukteshvara include him. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1]

Panigrahi called it the most decorated of the early temples that survive in fair condition. He noted carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Rajendralala Mitra described rows of horses and elephants carved on the porch hall. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,3]

Note: Mitra reads the lower porch panels as scenes from Rama's life; Panigrahi speaks of scenes from Shiva's life. They may describe different panels.

Mukteshvara Temple
Date
c. 966–975 CE Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [2,1]

Note: Percy Brown (1959) judged from details of its style that it was 'probably built about' 975 CE. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) argued for 966 CE. He took that year from a palm-leaf manuscript verse about a Shiva temple, and linked it to this temple through a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Panigrahi also places it between the Sisiresvara (c. 800 CE) and the Brahmesvara (c. 1060 CE). No inscription dates the temple. The research report's 'Brown c. 950' is not supported by Brown's text.

Dynasty
Somavamshi (Kesari) Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1]

Note: This is one scholar's view. Panigrahi bases it on the temple's style and on a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it, whom he identifies as the Somavamshi ruler Yayati I. Percy Brown (1959) dates the temple but names no dynasty in the passage checked. No inscription links the temple to a dynasty.

Height
about 10.5 m (35 ft) Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,1]

Note: Brown: the tower is 'hardly 35 feet high'. Panigrahi: 'a height of only 34' feet, with an unclear fraction in the scan text. Rajendralala Mitra (1880) gives 'barely 3S feet' (scan text unclear: 35 or 38). None of these is an ASI measurement.

Deity
Not yet verified — see our content policy.
Temple type
pancharatha shrine with pidha jagamohana Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1]

What's special

In front stands a free-standing gateway called a torana (arched gateway). Two carved pillars hold up a round arch. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,3,1]

Percy Brown called the arch one of the most original ideas in the whole Odisha style. In 1961, K.C. Panigrahi noted that no other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has such an arch. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,1]

Scholars have praised its beauty. Percy Brown called it 'a miniature gem of architecture'. James Fergusson wrote that, in its class, it was 'the gem of Orissan architecture'. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,4]
